answer.rationale: The two acute symptoms are onboarding completion (-4%) and activation (-6%), and onboarding sits upstream of activation, so fixing friction there plausibly addresses both. The competitor's entry pricing is the loudest signal but memory_73 is the one inherited record that carries explicit downstream harm: +31% new accounts and +18% booked revenue came with -12pp first-term renewals among price-sensitive buyers. Matching a price attack would buy exactly the cohort that already failed to renew, which is the opposite of sustainable qualified revenue. Referral (memory_57) and enterprise sales-assist (memory_44) are credible but address neither declining metric this quarter. I am spending verification on memory_86 and memory_31 rather than the pricing record because the pricing record already reports its own downside and does not need confirming, while the onboarding evidence has two weaknesses I cannot resolve from the summaries. First, both memories may trace to the same underlying experiment; if so my apparent two-source support collapses to one and the case weakens materially. Second, both are stated in proxy terms (completion rates, first-week activation, time-to-value) with no link to retained or qualified revenue, and 'durable lift' in memory_31 is unquantified with no stated horizon. Cutting required signup fields also has a specific downstream risk worth naming: fewer qualifying fields can raise activation counts while degrading lead quality and segmentation, which would show up as revenue harm well after the experiment window closes. So I will instrument for retained qualified revenue and lead quality, not completion rate alone. If the archive shows the two records share a source or that the lift was never measured past week one, I would drop to a small guarded test or shift the slot to activation_messaging (memory_91), which targets the larger decline but is the vaguest record in the set.
